# How to Give AI a Spreadsheet Export and Ask for Clean Summary Tables

> **In short:** Export your spreadsheet as a CSV (a plain-text table file), describe what each column means, then ask the AI for summary tables. Always check a few totals yourself, because AI can make arithmetic mistakes.

You already know how to start a chat and send a message. In this guide you will learn a more useful workflow: handing the AI a real data file, explaining it once, and asking for summary tables you can paste back into your spreadsheet app. This is for anyone who keeps lists of sales, expenses, class grades, volunteer hours, or inventory and wants a faster summary.

## Before you start
- An AI chat account you already use, and a way to attach a file in that chat. If you don't see an attachment option, you can still paste text, as Step 3 explains.
- A spreadsheet app with a table you want to summarize, such as Excel or Google Sheets.
- Time: about 30 minutes for the first run.
- Some assistants limit file size or file types, and some file-upload features may need a paid plan. Check your assistant's help center if an upload fails.

## Step 1 — Export your table as a CSV file
A CSV (comma-separated values) file is a plain-text version of a table. Each row is a line, and commas separate the cells. Almost every spreadsheet app can save one, which makes it easy for AI tools to read. Open your spreadsheet and look in the File menu, or in a menu with a similar name, for an option like Download or Save As. Choose CSV. Name the file something clear, such as "sales-march.csv".

Before you export, delete any blank rows, merge nothing, and make sure the first row holds short column headers like "Date," "Region," and "Amount." Remove private details such as full names, account numbers, or medical or financial records. Use initials or "Customer 1" instead.

You'll know it worked when you see a file in your downloads folder whose name ends in .csv, and it opens as plain text with commas between values.

## Step 2 — Describe your columns in plain words
AI can read a CSV, but it cannot guess what your columns mean. A column called "Q3" could mean a quarter, a score, or a code. Write a short description of each column so the AI reads your data the way you do. Think of it like handing a new coworker a labeled map before they start a project.

Write one line per column in a notes document. For example, "Date: the day the order was placed," or "Amount: the total in US dollars, before tax." Keep it to about one line per column.

💬 Example: "Here is what my columns mean. Date is the order day. Region is one of [North, South, East, West]. Amount is the order total in dollars before tax. Rep is the salesperson's first name."

If a column has codes, list them too, so the AI does not guess what they stand for.

You'll know it worked when every column in your file has a matching description in your notes.

## Step 3 — Share the file with your assistant
Start a new chat so the conversation stays clean. Look for an attachment button next to the message box, often a paperclip or a plus sign, and use it to upload your CSV. Then send your column descriptions in the same message. If you don't see an attachment option, open the CSV in a text editor, copy the header row and the first 20 rows, and paste them into the message box, with your column notes above them.

The AI usually reads the file and replies with a short confirmation of what it found, such as the number of rows and the column names. If it describes columns you don't recognize, your file may not have uploaded correctly. Try again with the pasted version.

💬 Example: "Please read the attached file and tell me how many rows it has, then list the column names you found. Use my column descriptions from my message."

You'll know it worked when the AI repeats your column names back to you accurately.

## Step 4 — Ask for summary tables with a reusable template
This is the step that makes the workflow reusable. Instead of a vague request like "summarize this," give a precise template you can save and reuse next month. Name the grouping you want, the totals or averages you need, and the format. Ask for a plain table with clear headers, because a clean table pastes into a spreadsheet with fewer problems.

Save your template in a note app. If your assistant offers projects or saved custom instructions, you can keep the template there so you don't retype it. If it does not, copy it from your notes each time.

💬 Example: "Create three summary tables from this file. Table 1: total Amount by Region, with a grand total row. Table 2: number of orders by Rep. Table 3: average Amount by month. Output each table as plain rows with a header line and no extra commentary."

If the answer comes back as paragraphs instead of a table, reply with "Please put each table in plain rows I can copy into a spreadsheet." Good answers usually take one or two rounds.

You'll know it worked when you see separate tables with headers and totals that match the grouping you asked for.

## Step 5 — Check the numbers before you trust them
AI tools can misread rows, skip a few, or make an arithmetic slip, especially with large files. The AI cannot promise exact totals, so you must verify. Pick the simplest number, like the grand total in Table 1. Use your spreadsheet's own SUM function or total row to calculate the same figure. If the two match, the table is likely right. If they don't, ask the AI to recount and show its work for one group.

It is also smart to check one small group by hand. Filter your spreadsheet to a single region and compare its count with the AI's count.

💬 Example: "Your grand total for Region seems off. Please recount the Amount column, list each region's subtotal separately, and then give the grand total."

You'll know it worked when the AI's grand total matches your spreadsheet's own total.

## Step 6 — Paste the tables back into your spreadsheet
Copy one table from the chat. Most chat windows let you select the table and copy it, or you can use a copy button that appears when you hover over the answer. Open a new sheet tab in your spreadsheet, click the cell where you want the table to start, and paste. If everything lands in one column, look for a paste option like "Paste special" or "Text to columns" and choose the option that splits text at commas or tabs. You may also need to ask the AI to output the table with commas instead of spaces.

Give each pasted table its own labeled area, and keep your original data on a separate tab so you never overwrite your source.

💬 Example: "Please reformat Table 1 as comma-separated values with one header row, so I can paste it into a spreadsheet and have each value land in its own column."

You'll know it worked when the summary table sits in clean columns in your spreadsheet and the headers are in the first row.

## Common mistakes
- **Uploading private data.** Names, account numbers, and health or money details should not go into any chat tool you don't control. Fix it by replacing identifying details with codes like "Customer 1" before exporting.
- **Skipping the column descriptions.** Without them, the AI guesses, and guesses produce wrong totals. Fix it by writing one line per column, as in Step 2.
- **Trusting the first answer.** A clean-looking table can still be wrong. Fix it by checking one total against your spreadsheet's own formula, as in Step 5.

## What this means for you
- **In everyday life:** Summarize a household budget export, a fitness log, or a book club list by month or category, then paste the result into a simple chart.
- **For your business or work:** Turn a weekly sales or inventory export into three standard summary tables for a Monday meeting, using the same saved template each week.
- **If you want to go further:** Ask the AI to compare this month's summary with last month's, by uploading two CSV files and writing a template that names both. Check the results the same way, and remember the AI cannot see formulas or charts inside your original file.

## Try it now
Export one small spreadsheet with fewer than 50 rows as a CSV. Write one-line descriptions for its columns, then ask your assistant for a single summary table with a grand total. Spend two minutes checking that total against your spreadsheet.
